structure.title: 3. Empirical framework (definitions, sample, outcomes, RD estimation, executive turnovers)
4. Main results (identification checks, main results, robustness, close vs other elections, leader characteristics)
Acknowledgments, Supplementary Data, Data Availability, References

observations.statement: The design is named as a close-elections regression discontinuity across countries with one observation per election; the estimand is the effect of an electoral defeat of the incumbent at the cutoff of the challenger's victory margin, estimated with the non-parametric method of Calonico et al. (2014).

The identifying assumption is stated as ex ante comparability of elections narrowly won by incumbents and challengers. Two endogeneity sources are laid out (unobservables correlated with reelection prospects; systematic differences between reelected and defeated incumbents), with an explicit note that the RD handles the first and only partly the second.

A dedicated interpretation subsection discusses local nature of the RD estimate: negatively selected incumbents and strong challengers in close races, and different incentives for closely versus decisively reelected incumbents, with the direction of implied bias spelled out before results are presented.

For executive turnovers a fuzzy RD is used: the executive turnover indicator is instrumented by the sign of a distinct running variable (margin over the pre-election leading party). The exclusion restriction is stated, flagged as unlikely to hold in some settings, and reduced-form estimates are reported alongside. The fuzzy, first-stage and reduced-form equations are placed in Appendix A.2.

The election universe is built from V-Dem as the primary source and complemented by many named election databases, books and archives; the unit is the national election (presidential or lower-chamber parliamentary) over a stated post-war period. Sources are prioritized by coverage, consistency and prior use.

When academic sources are lacking, results are collected from Wikipedia; the share of such cases is disclosed in a footnote, and an appendix figure compares the assembled sample with pre-existing databases and counts elections by source.

Exclusions are listed with reasons: unopposed candidates, non-final elections in a calendar year, manipulable indirect elections, inconsequential elections, powerless constitutional assemblies, partly appointed chambers, ties, and undefined incumbents. A footnote checks exclusion probability at the cutoff; an appendix table re-includes inconsequential elections.
observations.locator: Sections 3.1.1 and 3.1.2, footnote 9; Appendices A.1, A.3, Figure C.1, Table D.5

observations.statement: The key running and treatment variables were checked through an independent audit covering all elections within a narrow margin window plus a subset of other elections, documented in a data appendix.

Main tables report both the total number of observations and the number of observations inside the MSE-optimal bandwidth for each outcome; the heterogeneity table reports N only for the general-index row.
Outcome data coverage per outcome is tabulated in an appendix, and a separate appendix table checks that the fraction of observations with missing outcome data is not affected by treatment.
observations.locator: Section 2.2; Appendix Tables B.1 and C.1

observations.statement: Incumbency follows explicit rules (executive power held for a minimum number of days in a fixed pre-election window; previous-election seat plurality for parliaments), with rules for designated successors and ex ante versus ex post coalitions. Treatment is incumbent defeat; the running variable is the top challenger's margin, using run-off or electoral college shares where relevant.

Outcomes are defined as the difference between the average level over the post-election years and the pre-election year level, then standardized so estimates read in SD units; the post-window length is set to the modal inter-election distance.

Summary indices follow Kling et al. (2007): unweighted averages of standardized components, signed so higher is better, missing components omitted rather than imputed; an economic index and a general index nesting economic, human development and democracy. Economic components are winsorized at symmetric percentiles, with the outlier motivation stated.

Each economic outcome is tied to a named source (Penn World Tables version stated, IMF, ILO, World Bank), chosen for coverage of the election sample; human development from UNDP and democracy as the simple average of five V-Dem indices bounded on the unit interval.

The main table reports, per outcome column, the RD point estimate, robust standard error in parentheses, the p-value from the robust confidence interval in brackets, total N, effective N within the bandwidth, and the MSE-optimal bandwidth in percentage points; notes name the estimator and define each row.

The executive-turnover table stacks four panels per outcome: fuzzy RD second stage, reduced form, first stage, and OLS, each with its own N, effective N and bandwidth, with notes mapping panels to appendix equations.

The baseline RD includes no fixed effects or covariates; region and decade fixed effects and pre-election outcome controls are added only as robustness checks in the appendix, where the effect on precision is noted.
observations.locator: Equation (1); Section 4.3.3; Appendix Tables D.11-D.15, D.17

observations.statement: Inference uses the robust bias-corrected standard errors and confidence intervals of Calonico et al. (2014) as the default; clustering at the country by year level is presented only as an appendix robustness check in a footnote, without a stated rationale for the baseline choice of no clustering.

Multiple testing is addressed by aggregation rather than p-value correction: outcomes are grouped into summary indices to reduce overrejection and gain power, with explicit reference to the multiple-testing problem.
Randomization inference following Cattaneo et al. (2015) is reported as a robustness alternative to the conventional RD inference, placed in a dedicated appendix.

Differences between subsample estimates are tested with the Clogg et al. (1995) method, with p-values reported in the table notes, and a parametric interaction specification is mentioned as giving broadly consistent results.

The Cattaneo et al. (2018) density test is the first identification check: a main-text figure for the full sample and by election type, repeated in the appendix for regime types, free-and-fair status and small parliaments. A failure in one subsample is discussed, attributed to possible retrospective coding, and handled by a drop-that-subsample robustness table.
observations.locator: Section 4.1; Figure 3; Appendix Figure C.2; Tables D.7, D.8; footnote 14

observations.statement: Placebo tests regress pre-election outcome levels and year-on-year differences on treatment for several pre-election years; continuity is also checked for decade and region dummies, time since last treatment, the previous running variable and previous treatment. All are in the appendix and summarized in one main-text paragraph.
observations.locator: Section 4.1; Appendix Tables C.2-C.7, Figure C.3

observations.statement: Joint continuity of a large set of pre-election covariates at the cutoff is tested with the Canay and Kamat (2017) permutation test, for the full sample and several subsamples, reported in an appendix table.

The first stage for the fuzzy design is shown both as binned RD plots of executive turnover probability against the margin (parliamentary only and full sample) and as a table panel with estimates per outcome sample.
A dynamic RD estimates the effect separately for each post-election year and for a pre-election year; the pre-election coefficient is labelled a placebo in the figure and interpreted as such.

RD implementation checks are listed as five deviations from the Calonico et al. defaults: adding region and decade fixed effects and pre-election controls, halving and doubling the bandwidth, a second-order local polynomial, alternative kernels, and randomization inference. Main text gives a brief overview; tables are in the appendix.
observations.locator: Section 4.3.3; Appendix Tables D.11-D.17, Appendix F

observations.statement: Outcome-construction robustness covers alternative post-election window lengths, inclusion of the election year, a multi-year pre-election baseline, lighter and heavier winsorization, and trimming, each reported per outcome in appendix tables.

Index-construction robustness drops each component in turn, restricts to complete cases, uses a Pocock-type correlation-weighted index, averages all underlying outcomes, and drops each region and each decade; sample robustness restricts to major elections and excludes regime-change elections, all collected in one appendix table.

Alternative data sources for the same outcome (GDP growth, trade) and alternative democracy measures including real-time coded ones are used to check that results are not source-specific; sources are named in footnotes and appendix tables.
observations.locator: Section 2.2 footnote 7; Section 4.2 footnote 16; Section 4.3.7; Appendix Tables D.1-D.4

observations.statement: OLS estimates, described as difference-in-differences because outcomes are differenced from the pre-election year, are compared with RD estimates across nested windows around the cutoff in a coefficient figure, with an explicit statement that OLS lacks a causal interpretation.

Locality of the RD estimate is addressed with three exercises: OLS in wider windows, a subsample of elections made close by exogenous oil-price shocks, and the Angrist and Rokkanen (2015) conditional-independence approach with a testable CIA, linear reweighting and propensity-score estimators, and an equality test against the RD estimates.
observations.locator: Sections 4.4.1-4.4.3; Appendix Tables E.4, E.5; Figures E.5, E.6

observations.statement: The paper reports how close elections differ from the full sample in regime type, OECD membership and pre-election conditions, pointing to an appendix figure, so readers can judge the population to which the local estimate applies.

Heterogeneity uses split samples at the median of the moderator computed among close elections, estimating the RD separately in each half; three dimensions are in a main-text table, others (executive power, globalization exposure, regime, OECD, tenure, previous turnover) in appendix tables, and a coefficient plot shows many subsamples at once.
observations.locator: Section 4.2.1; Table 2; Figure 5; Appendix Tables E.1, E.3

observations.statement: Each heterogeneity split is preceded by a short statement of competing predictions, and the text comments on whether the difference across subsamples is statistically distinguishable rather than on the point estimates alone.

Policy change is tested first on directional policy levels and then on the absolute value of the post minus pre change, to capture non-directional shifts; the same RD is applied to many policy measures with a count of positive estimates reported as summary.
observations.locator: Section 3.4.1; Section 5.1; Appendix Figure E.7, Tables E.6, E.7

observations.statement: Accountability is probed with corruption and accountability indices, their dynamics over post-election years to address endogenous expert coding, an incident-based corruption measure, and a term-limits subsample; conclusions are labelled suggestive.
observations.locator: Section 5.2, 5.2.1; Appendix Figures E.9, E.10; Tables E.10, E.11, E.1

observations.statement: Leader characteristics as an alternative channel are examined by running the RD on winner ideology scores and on a constructed leader-quality proxy (change in vote share to next election, residualized on pre- and post-election performance), with a bounding exercise by prior government experience in a footnote.
observations.locator: Section 4.5; Appendix Figure E.8, Tables E.8, E.9; footnotes 23, 24

observations.statement: Four country case studies with time-series figures are used in an appendix to illustrate the main result, introduced by a short main-text subsection titled Examples.

Effects are expressed in standard deviation units of the differenced outcome throughout; estimates in natural units are provided in an appendix table and referred to appendix means and SDs for translation.
observations.locator: Introduction; Section 4.2; Appendix Tables D.10, B.3

observations.statement: The text distinguishes point estimates that are positive but not significant from significant ones, reports p-values inline for borderline cases, and compares fuzzy-RD executive-turnover magnitudes with electoral-turnover magnitudes while noting reduced precision from the smaller sample.
A dedicated paragraph acknowledges imperfect coverage across countries and years, heterogeneous measurement quality, and unobserved policy outcomes as inherent limits of a global dataset.

Expert-coded outcomes (democracy, corruption) are flagged as potentially influenced ex post by the occurrence of a turnover; the caveat is handled by alternative sources, real-time coded measures, non-electoral dimensions and dynamic patterns rather than dropped.

Small-sample and power caveats are stated for ideology regressions and for the subsample with differentially binding term limits; the leader-quality channel is acknowledged as not directly observable and therefore not fully excluded.

RD plots use sample means in fixed-width bins of the running variable with linear fits on each side, and print the RD estimate, robust confidence interval and robust p-value at the bottom of each panel; figure notes restate the sample and definitions.

Subsample results and dynamic effects are shown as coefficient plots with robust confidence intervals at a lower nominal level than the intervals printed on the RD plots; the level used is stated in each figure note.

Tables use significance stars with the threshold legend in notes (the main table omits the ten percent star, other tables include it); notes define the sample, estimator, running variable and each panel. Appendix material is lettered by topic: A equations and examples, B data, C identification checks, D robustness, E heterogeneity and mechanisms, F randomization inference, G case studies.

Descriptive figures precede results: the share of elections with a turnover per half-decade in the main text, and geographical distribution maps of identified, analysed and turnover elections in the appendix.

The introduction previews the main estimates, heterogeneity, mechanisms, and the identification checks, followed by contribution paragraphs positioned against several literatures and a one-paragraph roadmap. Data sources are described before the empirical framework.

Within results, identification checks come first, then the main table, heterogeneity, dynamics, fuzzy-RD executive turnovers, examples, a robustness subsection that only summarizes appendix tables, extrapolation beyond the cutoff, and leader characteristics; mechanisms form a separate section. Most robustness, placebo and mechanism tables live in a lettered appendix.

Variable definitions are made concrete with named historical elections showing the values of running and treatment variables under both the electoral and executive definitions, including a case where the two definitions disagree.
A Data Availability statement says data and code are publicly available on Zenodo with a DOI; supplementary data are said to be available at the journal site. No software is named in the main text.

All inputs are public databases, archives, books and online sources linked by the authors into a new election dataset, with linkage rules documented in lettered data appendices (elections, leaders, parties, regimes, election roles, term limits, outcomes, executive turnovers, incumbency).

Footnotes carry many pre-emptive checks (exclusion probability, small parliaments, prior free-and-fair elections, election timing, leader age and gender, alternative trade sources), each pointing to a specific appendix table or figure.

gaps: No stated rationale for the baseline choice of unclustered robust RD standard errors; clustering appears only as a footnoted appendix check.
No software or package names in the main text (rdrobust and rddensity appear only in the code).
No summary statistics table in the main text; means and SDs are in Appendix Table B.3.
No preregistration or ethics statement (observational data, none expected).
No bandwidth sensitivity plot in the main text; only the half and double bandwidth tables in the appendix are mentioned.
No placebo cutoff test mentioned; placebos are on pre-election outcomes and pre-election covariates.
Weights are never mentioned; baseline appears unweighted.

reading.note: All 34 pages of the published article were read, including the reference list on pages 32 to 34. The online appendix (Appendices A to I, Tables B to E, Figures C to G) is not part of the extracted text and was not read; appendix contents are recorded only as referenced from the main text.
